Frigid means intensely and uncomfortably cold. Not just a little chilly — think of the kind of cold that bites at your skin, makes your breath visible, and stops you in your tracks. It is a strong, emphatic word. Whenever you use it, you are saying that something is not merely cold, but severely, piercingly cold.

Frigid has two distinct areas of use — one literal (about actual temperature) and one figurative (about people and behavior).

Meaning 1 — Extremely Cold (Temperature)

This is the most direct, everyday meaning. It describes temperatures, climates, or physical environments that are bitterly and intensely cold.

Examples:

  • "The frigid Arctic wind cut right through her coat."
  • "The swimmers jumped into the frigid water and immediately gasped."
  • "January mornings in that city are absolutely frigid."

You will often see it describing:

  • Weather and climate — a frigid winter, a frigid night, frigid temperatures
  • Water — frigid ocean water, a frigid river
  • Places — a frigid landscape, a frigid room
  • Air — frigid air, a frigid breeze

How cold is "frigid" exactly?
There is no fixed number, but it always implies cold that is physically uncomfortable and difficult to endure. A cool autumn breeze is not frigid. A freezing mountain blizzard is. The word carries a sense of hostile coldness — cold that feels almost aggressive.

Meaning 2 — Cold, Stiff, and Unfriendly in Behavior or Personality

Here, frigid is used metaphorically. Just as frigid weather pushes people away and makes them uncomfortable, a frigid person or atmosphere does the same — emotionally. It describes someone (or a social situation) that is:

  • Unwelcoming
  • Emotionally cold and distant
  • Stiff, formal, and lacking any warmth
  • Showing little or no friendliness, affection, or enthusiasm

Examples:

  • "When I greeted her, she gave me a frigid stare and walked away."
  • "The meeting had a frigid atmosphere — nobody smiled, nobody joked."
  • "His frigid response to my apology made it clear he hadn't forgiven me."
  • "She was polite but frigid — you could tell she didn't really want to be there."

This usage is about emotional temperature, not physical temperature. When someone is described as frigid in this way, they are not being cruel or aggressive — they are simply giving off zero warmth. They may even be technically polite, but in a cold, robotic, detached way that feels uncomfortable.

Meaning 3 — Lacking Sexual Responsiveness (Sensitive Usage)

Frigid is also used to describe a person — historically almost always a woman — who is considered to be unresponsive to or uninterested in sexual intimacy. A frigid person in this sense appears emotionally and physically closed off in a romantic or sexual context.

Example:

  • "He accused her of being frigid because she didn't share his level of physical interest."

Important things to know about this usage:

  • This meaning has a long, loaded history. For decades, it was used to dismiss or shame women who were less sexually expressive or simply had different needs than their partners.
  • Modern understanding recognizes that labeling someone as frigid this way is often unfair and oversimplified — it ignores differences in desire, comfort, trauma, health conditions, and relationship dynamics.
  • As a result, this usage is now widely considered outdated, judgmental, and offensive, especially when applied to women.
  • You will still encounter it in older literature, films, and conversations — so it's important to recognize it — but using it yourself in this way is generally seen as unkind and reductive.
How Frigid Differs from Similar Words

WordWhat makes it different
ColdGeneral and neutral. Can mean mildly cold or unfriendly, but without the intensity of frigid.
FreezingAlso intense, but more casual and everyday. "I'm freezing!" is something you say casually; frigid sounds more deliberate and formal.
IcyVery close to frigid in both meanings. But icy often suggests sharpness or hostility (an icy glare = aggressive coldness), while frigid leans more toward blankness and absence of warmth rather than sharp hostility.
ChillyMuch milder than frigid, both literally and figuratively. A chilly room is just a little cold. A chilly person is slightly distant, not deeply closed off.
GlacialSimilar to frigid, but often used to emphasize slowness and immovability alongside coldness (a glacial pace, a glacial response).
The Overall Tone and Register of the Word

• Frigid is a formal-to-neutral word. It doesn't feel slang-like. You will hear it in writing, journalism, literature, and careful speech.
  • It almost always carries a negative connotation. Whether it's weather or personality, frigid describes something unwelcoming and uncomfortable.
  • It is an emphatic word — you reach for it when you want to communicate that the coldness is significant, not minor.

Frigid means:

  1. Intensely, harshly cold — used for weather, water, air, and physical environments.
  2. Emotionally cold, stiff, and deeply unfriendly — used for people, interactions, or atmospheres.
  3. Sexually unresponsive — an older, now largely considered offensive use, mostly applied to women; important to recognize but not to casually repeat.

In all three cases, the word communicates an absence of warmth — whether that warmth is physical heat, human kindness, or intimate connection.
